{{Short description|Maximum number of colors in a greedy graph coloring}}
{{about|greedy coloring of graphs|the system of arithmetic used in combinatorial game theory|nimber|the value of an impartial game|Sprague–Grundy theorem}}
[[File:Greedy colourings.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|An optimal greedy coloring (left) and Grundy coloring (right) of a [[crown graph]]. The numbers indicate the order in which the greedy algorithm colors the vertices.]]
In [[graph theory]], the '''Grundy number''' or '''Grundy chromatic number''' of an [[undirected graph]] is the largest number of colors in any [[greedy coloring]] of the graph. More precisely, it is the number of colors used by a [[greedy coloring]] strategy that considers the vertices of the graph in sequence and assigns each vertex its [[Mex (mathematics)|first available]] color, using a vertex ordering chosen to use as many colors as possible. Grundy numbers are named after [[Patrick Michael Grundy|P. M. Grundy]], who studied an analogous concept for [[directed graph]]s in 1939.<ref>{{citation|first=P. M.|last=Grundy|author-link=Patrick Michael Grundy|title=Mathematics and games|journal=[[Eureka (University of Cambridge magazine)|Eureka]]|volume=2|year=1939|pages=6–8|url=http://www.archim.org.uk/eureka/27/games.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927192024/http://www.archim.org.uk/eureka/27/games.html|archive-date=2007-09-27}}. ==Examples==
The [[path graph]] with four vertices provides the simplest example of a graph whose [[chromatic number]] differs from its Grundy number. This graph can be colored with two colors, but its Grundy number is three: if the two endpoints of the path are colored first, the greedy coloring algorithm will use three colors for the whole graph.<ref name="z"/>

The [[complete bipartite graph]]s are the only connected graphs whose Grundy number is two. All other connected graphs contain either a triangle or a four-vertex path, which cause the Grundy number to be at least three.<ref name="z"/>

The [[crown graph]]s are obtained from complete bipartite graphs <math>K_{n,n}</math> by removing a [[perfect matching]]. As a result, for each vertex on one side of the bipartition, there is exactly one vertex on the opposite side of the bipartition that it is not adjacent to. As bipartite graphs, they can be colored with two colors, but their Grundy number is <math>n</math>: if a greedy coloring algorithm considers each matched pair of vertices in order, each pair will receive a different color. As this example shows, the Grundy number can be larger than the chromatic number by a factor linear in the number of graph vertices.<ref>{{Citation
 | last= Johnson |first = D. S.
 | author-link= David S. Johnson
 | contribution= Worst-case behavior of graph coloring algorithms
 | mr = 0389644
 | title= Proc. 5th Southeastern Conf. on Combinatorics, Graph Theory, and Computing, Utilitas Mathematicae
 | place= Winnipeg
 | year= 1974 | pages= 513–527 }}</ref>

==Atoms==
{{harvtxt|Zaker|2006}}
defines a sequence of graphs called {{mvar|t}}-''atoms'', with the property that a graph has Grundy number at least {{mvar|t}} if and only if it contains a {{mvar|t}}-atom.
Each {{mvar|t}}-atom is formed from an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] and a {{math|(''t'' &minus; 1)}}-atom, by adding one edge from each vertex of the {{math|(''t'' &minus; 1)}}-atom to a vertex of the independent set, in such a way that each member of the independent set has at least one edge incident to it.
A Grundy coloring of a {{mvar|t}}-atom can be obtained by coloring the independent set first with the smallest-numbered color, and then coloring the remaining {{math|(''t'' &minus; 1)}}-atom with an additional {{math|''t'' &minus; 1}} colors.
For instance, the only 1-atom is a single vertex, and the only 2-atom is a single edge, but there are two possible 3-atoms: a triangle and a four-vertex path.<ref name="z"/>

==In sparse graphs==
For a graph with {{mvar|n}} vertices and [[degeneracy (graph theory)|degeneracy]] {{mvar|d}}, the Grundy number is {{math|''O''(''d'' log ''n'')}}. In particular, for graphs of bounded degeneracy (such as [[planar graph]]s) or graphs for which the [[chromatic number]] and degeneracy are bounded within constant factors of each other (such as [[chordal graph]]s) the Grundy number and chromatic number are within a logarithmic factor of each other.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Irani | first = Sandy
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01294263
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Algorithmica
 | mr = 1247988
 | pages = 53–72
 | title = Coloring inductive graphs on-line
 | volume = 11
 | year = 1994| s2cid = 181800
 }}.</ref> For [[interval graph]]s, the chromatic number and Grundy number are within a factor of 8 of each other.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Narayanaswamy | first1 = N. S.
 | last2 = Subhash Babu | first2 = R.
 | doi = 10.1007/s11083-008-9076-6
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Order
 | mr = 2395157
 | pages = 49–53
 | title = A note on first-fit coloring of interval graphs
 | volume = 25
 | year = 2008| s2cid = 207223738
 }}.</ref>

==Computational complexity==
Testing whether the Grundy number of a given graph is at least {{mvar|k}}, for a fixed constant {{mvar|k}}, can be performed in [[polynomial time]], by searching for all possible {{mvar|k}}-atoms that might be subgraphs of the given graph. However, this algorithm is not [[Parameterized complexity|fixed-parameter tractable]], because the exponent in its running time depends on {{mvar|k}}. When {{mvar|k}} is an input variable rather than a parameter, the problem is [[NP-complete]].<ref name="z">{{citation
 | last = Zaker | first = Manouchehr
 | doi = 10.1016/j.disc.2005.06.044
 | issue = 23
 | journal = [[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 2273147
 | pages = 3166–3173
 | title = Results on the Grundy chromatic number of graphs
 | volume = 306
 | year = 2006| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> The Grundy number is at most one plus the maximum degree of the graph, and it remains NP-complete to test whether it equals one plus the maximum degree.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Havet | first1 = Frédéric
 | last2 = Sampaio | first2 = Leonardo
 | contribution = On the Grundy number of a graph
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-17493-3_17
 | mr = 2770795
 | pages = 170–179
 | publisher = Springer, Berlin
 | series = Lecture Notes in Comput. Sci.
 | title = Parameterized and exact computation
 | volume = 6478
 | year = 2010| bibcode = 2010LNCS.6478..170H
 | isbn = 978-3-642-17492-6
 }}.</ref> There exists a constant {{math|''c'' > 1}} such that it is [[NP-hard]] under randomized reductions to [[approximation algorithm|approximate]] the Grundy number to within an [[approximation ratio]] better than&nbsp;{{mvar|c}}.<ref>{{citation|title=A lower bound for approximating Grundy numbering|first=Guy|last=Kortsarz|url=http://www.dmtcs.org/dmtcs-ojs/index.php/dmtcs/article/viewArticle/625|journal=Discrete Mathematics & Theoretical Computer Science|volume=9|issue=1|year=2007}}.</ref>

There is an exact [[exponential time]] algorithm for the Grundy number that runs in time {{math|''O''(2.443<sup>''n''</sup>)}}.<ref name="bfks"/>

For [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]], and [[partial k-tree|graphs of bounded treewidth]], the Grundy number may be unboundedly large.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Gyárfás | first1 = A.
 | last2 = Lehel | first2 = J.
 | doi = 10.1002/jgt.3190120212
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Journal of Graph Theory
 | mr = 940831
 | pages = 217–227
 | title = On-line and first fit colorings of graphs
 | volume = 12
 | year = 1988| s2cid = 8839035
 }}.</ref> Nevertheless, the Grundy number can be computed in polynomial time for trees,
and is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by both the [[treewidth]] and the Grundy number,<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Telle | first1 = Jan Arne
 | last2 = Proskurowski | first2 = Andrzej
 | doi = 10.1137/S0895480194275825
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics]]
 | mr = 1477655
 | pages = 529–550
 | title = Algorithms for vertex partitioning problems on partial {{mvar|k}}-trees
 | volume = 10
 | year = 1997}}.</ref> although (assuming the [[exponential time hypothesis]]) the dependence on treewidth must be greater than singly exponential.<ref name="bfks"/> When parameterized only by the Grundy number, it can be computed in fixed-parameter tractable time for [[chordal graph]]s and [[claw-free graph]]s,<ref name="bfks">{{citation
 | last1 = Bonnet | first1 = Édouard
 | last2 = Foucaud | first2 = Florent
 | last3 = Kim | first3 = Eun Jung | author3-link = Eun Jung Kim (computer scientist)
 | last4 = Sikora | first4 = Florian
 | contribution = Complexity of Grundy coloring and its variants
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-21398-9_9

 | title = Computing and combinatorics
 | volume = 9198

 | s2cid = 5514223
 }}.</ref> and also (using general results on [[subgraph isomorphism]] in [[sparse graph]]s to search for atoms)  for graphs of [[bounded expansion]].<ref name="bfks"/><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Dvořák | first1 = Zdeněk | author1-link = Zdeněk Dvořák
 | last2 = Kráľ | first2 = Daniel | author2-link = Daniel Kráľ

 | mr = 3024787

 | year = 2010| title-link = Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Nešetřil | first1 = Jaroslav | author1-link = Jaroslav Nešetřil
 | last2 = Ossona de Mendez | first2 = Patrice | author2-link = Patrice Ossona de Mendez
 | contribution = 18.3 The Subgraph Isomorphism Problem and Boolean Queries
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-27875-4

==Well-colored graphs==
{{main|Well-colored graph}}
A graph is called [[Well-colored graph|well-colored]] if its Grundy number equals its chromatic number. Testing whether a graph is well-colored is [[Co-NP-complete|coNP-complete]].<ref name="z"/> The [[Hereditary property|hereditarily]] well-colored graphs (graphs for which every [[induced subgraph]] is well-colored) are exactly the [[cograph]]s, the graphs that do not have a four-vertex path as an induced subgraph.<ref name="cs79"/>
